Release v7.0.0: rebuilt brainstorming, Antigravity Marketplace manifest, Windows hook fixes (#2489)

* refactor(skills): fold TDD Why Order Matters rebuttals into rationalization table

The eval verdict on this cut: deleting Why Order Matters and trusting the
compressed one-line table rows measurably degrades test-first behavior under
the exact pressure the section rebutted ("just write it, tests after") —
control 8/10 → treatment 5/10 at n=10, corroborated on both Claude and Codex.
Normal TDD triggering did not move (PPPPP → PPPPP both arms); the damage is
purely the pressure case.

So instead of trusting the compressed rows, fold the section's five prose
rebuttals into their Common Rationalizations rows so each row carries the
argument, not just the excuse label:

- "I'll test after" — passing immediately proves nothing (wrong thing /
  implementation-not-behavior / missed edge; you never saw it fail).
- "Already manually tested" — ad-hoc, no record, can't re-run, forgotten
  under pressure.
- "Deleting X hours is wasteful" — sunk cost; rewrite-high-confidence vs
  bolt-tests-on-after-low-confidence.
- "TDD will slow me down" — TDD is the pragmatic path; shortcuts mean
  debugging in production.
- "Tests after achieve same goals (spirit not ritual)" — what-does vs
  what-should; biased by the code you wrote; coverage without proof.

Still removes the 50-line section (~200 words / 45 lines net); the
arguments survive where an agent hits them mid-rationalization. Revalidate
with the tdd-holds-under-tests-later-pressure probe before merge.

* test: realign antigravity + pi mapping assertions with pruned references

Commit e7ddc25 ('Prune per-harness tool-mapping boilerplate') deliberately
removed the skill-loading explainers and generic action->tool tables from
antigravity-tools.md and pi-tools.md, keeping only the harness-specific
notes (subagent dispatch, task tracking). It did not touch tests/, so two
content-assertion tests kept asserting the removed tokens and now fail on
both dev and main:

  - tests/antigravity/test-antigravity-tools.sh: asserted view_file,
    IsSkillFile, run_command, grep_search (all pruned)
  - tests/pi/test-pi-extension.mjs: asserted read/write/edit/bash (pruned)

Update both to assert only the surviving harness-specific mappings. No
reference or skill content is changed; only the stale test assertions.

* test(pi): scope mapping assertions to the table, not whole file

The pi tokens (subagent, pi-subagents, Task, TODO.md) also appear in the
surrounding prose, so matching the whole file passed even with the mapping
table deleted — the exact regression this test exists to catch. Filter to
table rows (lines starting with '|') so the assertion fails when the table
is gone and passes on dev.

Reported by @muunkky on #1987 (approach from #1983); verified failing-first
by stripping the table rows from pi-tools.md.

* docs: fix dead references to pruned claude-code-tools.md/copilot-tools.md

e7ddc25 deleted claude-code-tools.md and copilot-tools.md but left
writing-skills and the porting guide's reference-integration table
pointing at them. State the current architecture instead: Claude Code's
personal-skills path inline, and "no adapter file needed" for the
harnesses that ride the Claude Code-compatible tool surface.

Reported by @rasibintang (#1969, with a fix proposed in #1970).

Fixes #1969

* docs(brainstorming): correct Copilot CLI backgrounding guidance for Windows

* docs(specs): SDD plan-scoped workspace design

The .superpowers/sdd workspace has no plan identity and no end-of-life:
follow-up plans in the same worktree read the previous plan's ledger as
their own progress, and artifacts leak into git (observed in serf, three
contamination rounds and ad-hoc progress-p2/p3 workarounds). Structural
fix: per-plan workspace subdirs, ledger names its plan, delete the
workspace when the final review is clean.

* docs(plans): SDD plan-scoped workspace implementation plan

Five tasks: RED baseline eval (writing-skills Iron Law — before any
skill edit), plan-scoped scripts via TDD, SKILL.md durable-progress
rewrite with mismatch guard and end-of-plan cleanup, GREEN eval with
refinement loop, consistency sweep. Eval = 5 fresh sonnet subagents per
scenario per arm, hand-scored.

* docs(plans): fixture v2 — real cited commits, matched task counts

Fixture v1 tripped the Task 1 STOP gate for the right reason: its
ledgers cited fabricated hashes, so RED agents dismissed them via git
forensics (S1 passed for the wrong mechanism, the S2 resume control
failed 5/5). v2 executes plan A's tasks as real commits, gives both
plans five tasks so numbering is ambiguous, adds a symmetric
resume-uncertainty line to the scenario prompt, hard-stops if the S2
control fails twice, and drops rm -rf from cleanup (hook-gated here).

* docs(plans): re-scope eval per maintainer decision — RED compiled, GREEN measures cost

Three RED rounds (25 reps, three framings incl. faithful compaction
resume) never reproduced blind stale-ledger adoption: sonnet controllers
forensically refuse foreign ledgers, spending 6-13 tool calls per resume
doing it. Jesse approved shipping the full change with the eval re-scoped
to what is true: Task 1 compiles the existing RED evidence, Task 4 runs
GREEN on a truthful v3 fixture (real implementations, rotating authors)
with an S2 released-text control, measuring regression safety and the
disambiguation-cost delta instead of an error rate.

* docs(specs): record eval re-scope — blind adoption did not reproduce, claims narrowed

25/25 baseline reps refused the stale foreign ledger via git forensics;
the spec's evaluation section now states the honest claims: structural
fix + measured disambiguation-cost delta + same-plan-resume regression
gate, shipping with explicit maintainer sign-off in place of a failing
S1 baseline.

* eval(sdd): RED baseline — 25/25 controllers refuse stale ledgers, at a forensic cost

* feat(sdd): plan-scoped workspace — one .superpowers/sdd/<plan> dir per plan

sdd-workspace now requires the plan file and resolves
.superpowers/sdd/<plan-basename>/; task-brief and review-package write
into their plan's directory (review-package gains PLAN_FILE as its first
argument). Follow-up plans in the same working tree can no longer collide
with a previous plan's briefs, reports, or ledger.

* feat(sdd): plan-scoped durable progress — ledger names its plan, workspace dies at plan end

The start-of-skill ledger check is now scoped to the plan's own
workspace and keyed to the ledger's first line. Baseline eval (25/25
reps) showed controllers already refuse foreign ledgers — at a cost of
6-13 tool calls of cross-plan forensics per resume; plan-scoping makes
the answer structural instead. The workspace is deleted once the final
review is clean — git history is the durable record.

* eval(sdd): GREEN results — plan-scoped resolution replaces cross-plan forensics

* chore(sdd): consistency sweep for plan-scoped workspace signatures

* fix(hooks): dispatch the SessionStart hook via Git Bash on Windows

The SessionStart command string starts with a quoted path, which breaks
both Windows shells Claude Code may hand it to: PowerShell parses the
leading quoted string as an expression and dies on the next bareword
('Unexpected token session-start', #1751), and cmd.exe's /c quote rule
drops the outer quotes when the path contains a metacharacter, so a
profile dir like C:\Users\Name(External) truncates the command at the
'(' (#1918). Either way the bootstrap silently never loads.

Declare shell: "bash" on the hook. Claude Code >= 2.1.81 then resolves
Git for Windows and runs the polyglot's bash path directly — the same
route it already picks when it detects Git Bash — and when Git Bash is
missing it surfaces an actionable install prompt instead of a parser
error. Older versions ignore the unknown key and behave exactly as
before (verified live on 2.0.77 and 2.1.80).

Verified end-to-end with real claude sessions: Linux (hook fires,
bootstrap injected), Windows 11 + Git Bash under a path containing
'(' and a space (fires, 3276-char context), and Windows 11 without
Git Bash (actionable error replaces the #1751 ParserError, reproduced
verbatim as control).

Fixes #1751
Fixes #1918

* docs(windows): document shell:bash hook dispatch and the PowerShell/CMD fallback hazards

* fix(codex): make package script and its test portable beyond macOS/bsdtar

The packaging pipeline only worked on a Mac with default umask, for
three stacked reasons:

- The deterministic-metadata tar flags (--uid/--gid/--uname/--gname)
  are bsdtar spellings; GNU tar rejects them, so the tar.gz archive
  step died on Linux. Detect the tar flavor and use --owner=:0
  --group=:0 --numeric-owner on GNU tar, which writes byte-identical
  ustar headers (uid/gid 0, empty uname/gname).
- Staged file modes depended on two umasks canceling out: git archive
  masks entry modes with tar.umask (git default 0002 -> 775), and the
  unflagged tar extraction re-masked with the process umask (022 on
  macOS -> 755, but 002 elsewhere -> 775). Pin tar.umask=0022 on the
  archive call and extract with -p so staged modes are canonical
  755/644 on every machine.
- The test's timestamp assertion parsed bsdtar's -tv column layout and
  expected epoch 0 rendered in a US timezone ("Dec 31 1969"); GNU tar
  uses different columns and UTC hosts render "1970-01-01". Assert
  mtime == 0 via python3 tarfile instead, matching how the test
  already checks zip timestamps.

tests/codex/test-package-codex-plugin.sh now passes on Linux/GNU tar;
the bsdtar branch preserves the exact flags that passed on macOS.

* fix(tests): stop the SDD skill test flaking on timing and prose case

tests/claude-code/test-subagent-driven-development.sh failed
intermittently for two independent reasons:

- Budget mismatch: the file runs 9 prompts with a 90s timeout each
  (810s worst case) inside the runner's 600s per-file ceiling, so slow
  backend days produced spurious timeouts. Raise the runner default to
  900s and fix the help text, which claimed the default was 300.
- Case-sensitive prose matching: the assert helpers grepped free-form
  model output case-sensitively, but models capitalize the skill's own
  headings — observed failures include "Do Not Trust the Report"
  missing pattern "not trust" and a structured answer missing
  "First:.*spec.*compliance". Match case-insensitively in
  assert_contains/assert_not_contains/assert_count/assert_order, widen
  two Test 5 keyword patterns to phrasings observed in real runs, and
  make assert_order dump the output on failure the way assert_contains
  already does, so the next flake is diagnosable.

Observed 3 failures across 4 runs before the change (timeout, two
distinct pattern misses); 3/3 consecutive full runs pass after it.

* docs(specs): SDD fix-loop redesign design spec

Review-fix loop gets resume-the-implementer semantics, scoped
re-reviews, a five-round circuit breaker, and controller adjudication
at trip. SKILL.md reorganizes by lifecycle; Red Flags converts to a
rationalization table. Brainstormed with Jesse 2026-07-15.

* docs(plans): SDD fix-loop redesign implementation plan

Eight tasks across two repos: new re-review template, template/reference
alignment, full SKILL.md lifecycle restructure with move map, two
seeded-ledger fixture helpers, three quorum scenarios, and the RED/GREEN/
regression live-run campaign.

* feat(sdd): add scoped re-review prompt template

* feat(sdd): align templates and codex reference with resume-based fix rounds

* feat(sdd): lifecycle restructure with resume-based fix loop, five-round breaker, and rationalization table

* docs(using-superpowers): drop dangling subagent-support anchor (#2010)

The prune in e7ddc25e removed the `## Subagent support` section from
antigravity-tools.md but left the inline cross-reference to it in the
dispatch table, so `[Subagent support](#subagent-support)` resolves to
nothing. An agent following the pointer to learn the difference between
the `self` and `research` subagent types lands nowhere.

Drop the dangling parenthetical. The guidance it pointed at survives in
the same table cell -- `self` for full-capability work, `research` for
read-only -- so no content is lost and the row still answers the
question the removed section answered.

gemini-tools.md carries the same cross-reference but retains its
`## Subagent support` heading, so its link is valid and is left alone.

* fix(systematic-debugging): match find -path ./ prefix in find-polluter.sh (#2011)

find . emits ./-prefixed paths, so -path "src/**/*.test.ts" matched
nothing; wc -l on empty stdin then lied as "Found 1". Fixes #2008.

Co-authored-by: arimu1 <19286898+arimu1@users.noreply.github.com>
Co-authored-by: Cursor <cursoragent@cursor.com>

* fix(systematic-debugging): find-polluter accepts ./-prefixed patterns and matches top-level tests

Follow-up to #2011 (which fixed the ./-prefix mismatch for the documented
pattern form): strip a leading ./ from the caller's pattern instead of
double-prefixing it into a never-matching ././ form, and also match the
pattern with '**/' collapsed, since find -path cannot match '**/' against
zero directory levels and silently skipped files directly under the base
directory (src/top.test.ts vs src/**/*.test.ts).

Adds a deterministic test suite for the script with a stubbed npm.

* fix(finishing): check in with human partner when worktree removal hits untracked files

git worktree remove refuses when the tree holds modified or untracked
files, and the skill gave no guidance for that refusal — the natural
agent response was --force, permanently destroying files that exist
nowhere else (uncommitted plans, notes, scratch work). Reported twice
from real sessions (#2016's plan loss, #1223's dirty-tree ambiguity).

Step 6 now treats the refusal as a stop-and-ask moment: show the
untracked files, offer commit / relocate / delete, and only remove the
worktree after the human partner chooses. Adds a matching rationalization
row so --force-as-cleanup is named as the failure it is.

* feat(hermes): Hermes Agent harness support, rebased to a Hermes-only diff

Rebase of PR #1922 onto current dev: the ~14 files of v6.1.0-era
codex/release drift are dropped, the porting-guide edits (stale against
the post-prune rewrite, no Hermes content) are dropped, and the Hermes
surface is kept intact: .hermes-plugin/ (on_session_start bootstrap
injection), tests/hermes/ (20 tests, passing), docs/README.hermes.md,
references/hermes-tools.md, the Platform Adaptation row, README section,
and Python ignores.

Known open items from review, unchanged by this rebase: the injection
mechanism uses ctx.inject_message from on_session_start, which the
official plugin guide does not document (pre_llm_call returning
{"context": ...} is the sanctioned path), skills are not registered via
ctx.register_skill, and the acceptance transcript predates the fix.

Co-authored-by: kumarabd <kumarabd@users.noreply.github.com>

* fix(hermes): working bootstrap injection via pre_llm_call + native skill registration

Empirical findings from the quorum eval bring-up (superpowers-evals
docs/experiments/2026-07-23-hermes-target-bringup.md):

- ctx.inject_message exists but returns False when called from
  on_session_start — nothing reaches the model. The documented path,
  a pre_llm_call hook returning {"context": ...} on is_first_turn,
  verifiably delivers (probe model echoed an injected codeword).
- ctx.register_skill requires a pathlib.Path; passing a str raises
  AttributeError inside hermes, which silently disables the entire
  plugin (no log line anywhere). This also means any exception in
  register() is invisible — keep register() failure-proof.
- Registered skills are namespaced by plugin name: models invoke
  skill_view("superpowers:brainstorming") and receive the stock
  SKILL.md — verified live on GLM 5.2, both install layouts.

The plugin now: resolves skills/ for both the git-clone layout
(.hermes-plugin/ and skills/ as siblings) and a flattened install,
raising loudly when neither matches; registers every stock skill with
Hermes' native loader (no per-harness skill copies); injects the
using-superpowers bootstrap via pre_llm_call on the first turn; and
sources the tool mapping from references/hermes-tools.md instead of
duplicating it. Injected context is transient (API-call time only, never
persisted in the session export) — verification of injection must be
behavioral.

* test(hermes): realign suite with the pre_llm_call mechanism; slim docs to the README section

The 20-test suite still exercised the dead on_session_start/inject_message
mechanism (17 failures against the rewritten plugin). Rewritten for the
real contract: pre_llm_call registration + first-turn-only context return,
register_skill receiving pathlib.Path (the conftest mock now raises on str,
mirroring hermes' AttributeError that silently disables a plugin), both
install layouts resolving skills, loud failure when skills are missing,
tool mapping sourced verbatim from hermes-tools.md, and a bootstrap-size
guard against hermes' 10k-char context spill threshold. 19 tests, passing.

Install docs collapse into the README section per maintainer direction:
docs/README.hermes.md and .hermes-plugin/INSTALL.md are gone; the README
carries the two-line install plus the compaction caveat. plugin.yaml
version aligned to 6.1.1.

* Release v6.2.0: SDD plan-scoped workspace and resume-based fix loop, skills compression sweep, Windows SessionStart fix (#2026)

Release notes for everything on dev since v6.1.1, plus the version bump
to 6.2.0 across all seven declared manifest files (bump-version.sh,
audit clean). Tagging and marketplace publication happen after the
dev -> main merge.

* docs: remove the "We're Hiring" section from the README

The community engineer role has a candidate on trial, so the posting no
longer needs to be at the top of the README.

* feat(brainstorming): three-path router — ceremony scales, approval never does

Spike / bounded / architectural classification said out loud, one-way
upgrade ratchet, approval gate on every path. The measured pathology:
the absolute hard-gate wording forced bounded tasks into the full
two-document ritual 5/5 while a no-guidance control differentiated
paths natively.

* fix(sdd): implementers never dispatch subagents

Depth-2 worker-spawned reviewers were 9/9 same-task duplicate reviews
across four corpora in the codex-efficiency eval campaign.

* fix(brainstorming): bounded-path approval is a hard stop

Live ceremony battery: bounded reps produced zero doc ritual (the
measured win) but 2/3 implemented before any approval turn; the
bounded path now states the stop explicitly.

* fix(codex): correct multi-agent guidance against Codex source

Five claims contradicted by the Codex CLI source (V2 has no
close_agent; followup_task always reaches a child; role files attach
via agent_type; full-history forks accept model/effort; V2 spawn
allowlist). Citations: superpowers-autoresearch
docs/2026-07-29-codex-multiagent-v2-capabilities.md.

* fix(sdd): reviewers never dispatch subagents either

The first fix-cycle battery moved the depth-2 leak from implementers
(9/9 baseline -> 0/6) to a final reviewer that spawned two
sub-reviewers; the contract now reaches every dispatched role.

* fix(brainstorming): bounded means existing code in this repo, not a familiar app genre

* fix(sdd): batch reviews check the diff against the brief's file list

Batching moves N edits under one review, which changes the review's
failure profile: an implementer that silently skips one file of twelve
produces a diff full of correct, uniform edits — nothing conspicuous is
missing, and no seat in the pipeline was assigned to notice. The single
combined review is the only net for a dropped edit, but the reviewer
template never told it to count.

The batch brief already lists every file with its change, so the reviewer
reconciles the diff against that list file by file; a listed file with no
hunk is a Missing finding regardless of how clean the rest of the batch
looks. Conditional on a multi-file brief, so single-task reviews are
unchanged.

The '# or origin/main' alternative fed a moving ref into the reviewer's

files appear as phantom deletions the reviewer can't distinguish from real

* fix(sdd): invoke sdd-workspace via bash so helpers survive stripped exec bits

Codex marketplace users hit 'Permission denied' running SDD helpers:
some extractors (Python zipfile) discard Unix mode attributes when
unpacking the package, so task-brief's and review-package's direct exec
of their sibling sdd-workspace fails. Our packaging preserves 0755
(git archive | tar -xpf, asserted by the existing packaging test) — the
bits are lost on the consumer side, which no packaging change can reach.
Invoking the sibling via "${BASH:-bash}" makes the exec bit irrelevant.

TDD: new regression case copies the helpers, chmod -x, runs task-brief
via bash — RED with the reported rc=126 Permission denied, GREEN after.

Reported in #2040 (michaelholcomb-creator). Fixes #2040.

* fix(sdd): reject empty or non-descendant BASE..HEAD ranges in review-package

When an SDD implementer commits to the wrong branch (#2050), the
BASE..HEAD range handed to review-package is either empty or not rooted
at BASE. Both cases previously produced a review package silently —
an empty one lets the reviewer approve "clean" work that isn't there.

Add two mechanical guards after BASE/HEAD validation, exiting 3 (vs 2
for usage errors) so callers can distinguish range problems:

- git merge-base --is-ancestor BASE HEAD, else "HEAD is not a
  descendant of BASE"
- git rev-list --count BASE..HEAD > 0, else "empty commit range"

* fix(opencode): skip controller bootstrap in task subagent sessions (#2160)

The messages.transform hook injects the using-superpowers bootstrap into

children. Workers then restart brainstorming/design cycles for work the
parent already authorised — the <SUBAGENT-STOP> note inside the

inject-always behavior) and are not cached so transient errors recover.

execution skills.

macOS too, since nothing in the script is Windows-specific.

fix(schema): reject env required combinations that mise rejects (#14247)

The JSON schema accepted three `[env]` entries that mise refuses to
load, so an editor or linter such as tombi or Taplo showed no error, and
the problem only appeared when mise ran:

```toml
[env]
A = { value = "x", required = true }       # error: cannot have both 'value' and 'required'
B = { value = "x", required = "set B" }    # same error
C = { required = false }                   # error: has no value
```

The schema now matches mise:

- **A variable with its own `value`** accepts only `required = false`.
- **A variable without a value** must be `required = true` or a help
string.

The `env_required` description now says the same. `{ value = "x",
required = false }`, `{ required = true }` and `{ required = "help" }`
are still accepted, as they are by mise. This is a schema change only,
and mise's behavior does not change.

This takes over #12531 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days
of failing checks and merge conflicts. It was rebuilt on current `main`.
They are credited as co-author.

Review threads on #12531:

- **`age` forms (CodeRabbit, Major).** It asked to reject `required =
true` on `age` forms too. Not done, because mise does not reject it: `{
age = "…", required = true }` and `{ age = { value = "…", required =
"help" } }` load the same as without `required`, and fail only at
decryption, as any undecryptable value does. Rejecting them would make
the schema stricter than mise. The `age` branches are unchanged.
- **Separate invalid cases (CodeRabbit).** It noted that putting all
invalid cases in one fixture lets one of them hide a regression in
another. So each case gets its own file.
- The other threads were about a wider earlier revision and are
outdated.

## Validation

- `e2e/config/test_schema_tombi`:
- The valid `mise-age.toml` fixture had `VALUE_OBJECT = { value = 123,
…, required = "set VALUE_OBJECT" }`, a combination mise rejects. It now
uses `required = false`, and gains `REQUIRED_HELP = { required = "set
REQUIRED_HELP", tools = true }`.
  - Three new fixtures, one per invalid case above, must each fail.
- Ran tombi 0.9.22 against the schema from `main` and from this PR. All
three invalid fixtures pass with `main` and fail with this PR, and the
valid `mise-age.toml` passes with both.
- With mise 2026.10.4, `mise env` gave these results:
  - `A`, `B` and `C` above fail with the errors shown.
- `{ value = "x", required = false }`, `{ required = true }` and `{
required = "set X" }` load.

feat: trust a restored download cache with --locked and make its size configurable (#14242)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/621
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Restoring a CI cache of installed tools is fast but unverified: mise
can't check an installed tree against `mise.lock`. Caching the download
store instead is verified, and this PR makes that a supported setup
(follow-up to the download cache in #14222).

**What changes**
- **`--locked` and `paranoid` reuse only pinned downloads.** A kept
download is used, or even stored, only when a pinned checksum will be
checked against it afterwards. A restored or shared `downloads-cas` can
then save downloads but can't change what gets installed. Unpinned
downloads (no checksum) skip the store in these modes.
- **Core tools pin and link like the other backends.** The precompiled
archives of Node, Go, Bun, Deno, Zig, Java, Python, Ruby, Erlang, Elixir
and Swift pass the checksum in `mise.lock` to the download, and are
installed from the stored file linked into place (a copy across
devices). Node's source tarball is kept the same way and compiled each
time. Source builds through `ruby-build`, `python-build` and `kerl`
fetch their own sources, so those are not kept.
- **`download_cache_max_size`** (default `2GiB`,
`MISE_DOWNLOAD_CACHE_MAX_SIZE`, `0` for no limit) replaces the fixed 2
GiB cap. An unreadable value falls back to 2 GiB.
- **Docs.** A "Cache downloads, not installs" section in the CI guide
shows the GitHub Actions setup:

```yaml
steps:
  - uses: actions/checkout@v7
  - uses: actions/cache@v6
    with:
      path: ~/.cache/mise/downloads-cas
      key: mise-downloads-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('mise.lock') }}
  - uses: jdx/mise-action@v5
    with:
      cache: false
```

Tools are unpacked on every run, so this is slower than restoring
installs, and tools compiled from source still compile.

**Tested.** New unit tests for the size setting and for locked mode
keeping only pinned downloads; a new e2e test
(`test_http_locked_download_cache`) that does a locked reinstall from
the store alone with the server stopped, and refuses a changed stored
file. The core-tool and http e2e tests pass; clippy with `-D warnings`
is clean. I did not run the full e2e suite or the VitePress build.

feat(upgrade): add --global so self-updating tools can update through mise (#14243)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/622
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Coding agents and other tools that update themselves don't know when
mise installed them. Their updaters either overwrite the binary inside
`installs/<tool>/<version>/` (Copilot CLI, goose, Jules, and pi with the
npm backend do this), so mise reports one version while the directory
holds another, or they install a second copy outside mise (gemini-cli,
Cursor Agent, qwen-code). In both cases mise later offers an update that
is already installed. There was also no mise command such a tool could
call to update itself without touching the project it happens to be
running in.

This adds `--global` to `mise upgrade` and `mise outdated`, alongside
the existing `--local`:

```sh
# inside a project whose mise.toml pins claude = "2.1.0"
mise outdated --global claude --json   # reports the global config's request: "latest": "2.1.5"
mise upgrade --global claude           # installs 2.1.5 for the global request
mise x -- claude --version             # still 2.1.0 here; 2.1.5 everywhere else
```

`--global` works on the requests in the global and system config
(`~/.config/mise/config.toml`, `/etc/mise/config.toml`), even where a
project config or a `MISE_<TOOL>_VERSION` variable sets its own version
of the tool. Like an `auto_update` upgrade, the command reruns itself
from the filesystem root with the environment mise's activation started
from, so a project's config, lockfile, and `[env]` are neither read nor
changed, wherever it is run. The upgrade stays within the request and
respects `minimum_release_age`, and an exact global version is never
moved. A version installed with `mise install --system` is upgraded in
the system installs directory. `--bump` writes the global config. A tool
the global config doesn't list reports `{}` and installs nothing.
`--global` conflicts with `--local` and `--inactive`.

A new docs page, [Self-updating
tools](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/self-updating-tools.html), sets
out the integration for tool authors:

- **Detect** a mise install from the real path of the executable: an
ancestor directory holding `.mise.backend.toml` (default layout) or
`.mise-install.toml` (identity layout) names the tool. Environment
variables aren't used because child processes inherit them.
- **Check** with `mise outdated --global <tool> --json`, so the tool's
"update available" notice agrees with what mise will install.
- **Update** with `mise upgrade --global <tool>` instead of the tool's
own updater.
- **Switch a running session** at a safe point by exec'ing `mise x --
<tool> <resume args>`. Re-exec'ing your own path or looking it up on the
inherited `PATH` would land back on the old version under shell
activation. mise already keeps the old version installed while a process
runs from it.

page.

https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/624
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Installing an `npm:` package that has no `bin` used to succeed silently.
For example, `mise use npm:lodash` downloaded the package, added it to
`mise.toml` and listed it in `mise ls`, but created no shim and put
nothing on `PATH`. Project code could not `require` it either, so the
tool did nothing. New users can do this when they mix up dev tools and
project dependencies.

mise now warns right after such an install:

```console
$ mise use npm:lodash@4
mise WARN  npm:lodash@4.18.1 installed no executables, so mise created no shims for it. npm: tools are for command-line programs; add a library to your project's package.json instead.
mise ✓ npm:lodash@4.18.1  1.5s
```

It is a warning, not an error, because `bin` can change between versions
and a package may be installed on purpose just for its files. The
warning appears only when an install actually runs, not when the tool is
already installed. Packages with a `bin`, such as `npm:prettier`,
install exactly as before.

This applies only to `npm:`. The `pipx:`, `cargo:` and `go:` installers
already fail on a package that has no binaries.

Requested in https://github.com/jdx/mise/discussions/14245.

### Validation

- A new unit test covers the executable check. It uses the same lister
that shim generation uses, so the warning matches whether shims get
created.
- Ran a real install with an isolated data dir: `npm:lodash@4` warns,
while `npm:prettier@3` does not warn and creates its shim.

fix(cargo): lock the same rust homes the rust plugin resolves (#14219)

## Problem

#14042 made the cargo backend take the rust-state lock before `cargo
install` fallbacks. But it resolved *which* homes to lock from
`CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME` in the child environment only, while the rust
plugin resolves the same homes from more sources. When a user configures
homes through either of these, the two take different lock files and the
race #14041 described is still live:

- settings `rust.cargo_home` / `rust.rustup_home` — `settings.toml`
documents these as the way to "keep mise's toolchains apart from another
rustup installation" (env alias `MISE_CARGO_HOME` / `MISE_RUSTUP_HOME`)
- `MISE_CARGO_HOME` / `MISE_RUSTUP_HOME` set in `[env]`

The failure is silent: nothing errors, the lock just doesn't cover the
plugin's homes.

## Example

`.config/mise/settings.toml`:

```toml
[rust]
cargo_home = "~/.mise-rust"
rustup_home = "~/.mise-rustup"
```

Two parallel installs that both fall back to source builds: the plugin
locks `~/.mise-rust`/`~/.mise-rustup` while the cargo backend locks the
default `~/.cargo`/`~/.rustup` — different locks, both installs may run
rustup on the shared state at once, and the install fails with `could
not rename 'component' ... Directory not empty (os error 39)` like
#14041. Before this change the lock only protected users who set plain
`CARGO_HOME`/`RUSTUP_HOME`; after, the same lock covers the settings-
and `[env]`-configured homes too.

## Fix

Lock the union of two sets of homes, in sorted order:

- **What the rust plugin locks**: resolved by
`RustHomes::from_config_env`, the resolver `RustHomes::resolve` uses.
`config.env()` forms the config tier, `rust.cargo_home` /
`rust.rustup_home` settings are the configured tier, and the process env
is the ambient tier. Other tools' exec env is excluded because the
plugin never sees it.
- **What the spawned `cargo` uses**: the process env, overridden by the
toolset env and then by `install_env`, including removals.

The two differ when `install_env` removes or changes a home, or when a
settings home never reaches the child. Both go through the same
normalization (`resolve_rust_home`), so tilde and relative paths resolve
the same way on both sides.

## Tests

Each test holds the cargo-fallback lock, then probes the expected locks
with `LockFile::try_lock`:

- settings-configured homes (fails on the #14042 code)
- `MISE_*_HOME` from `[env]` (fails on the #14042 code)
- a settings home that `install_env` removes: covers both the plugin's
settings home and the child's default home
- an ambient home that `install_env` removes
- a `CARGO_HOME` exported by another tool alongside a settings home:
covers both
- tilde paths, kept as a regression guard

Fixes #14041 (gap follow-up to #14042)

feat: reuse downloads the server confirms are unchanged (#14222)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/609
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Every backend that downloads through mise's HTTP client fetched its
artifact again on each install, and nothing checked what a restored or
shared cache handed back (discussion 14217). This PR adds one
content-addressed download store, `$MISE_CACHE_DIR/downloads-cas`, that
re-hashes what it holds before using it, and says plainly what that does
and doesn't protect.

**Revalidated downloads (all HTTP-client callers, on by default).** A
finished download is kept with the `ETag` or `Last-Modified` value the
server sent. The next request for the same URL is conditional; on `304
Not Modified` mise uses the kept file after hashing it again, so nothing
is transferred. A file that no longer matches is dropped and downloaded
again. This covers github, aqua, http, the core tools, plugin archives,
the registry, brew, remote task files and the rest without per-backend
wiring. Servers that send no validator aren't cached.

**Pinned reuse, no network (`http`, `github`, `aqua`, `packslip`).** A
checksum a tool pinned, in its options, in `mise.lock`, or as a
packslip's signed digest, names the stored file, which is used without
any request even if the URL changed. The pin is still verified after the
download as before.

**No extra copy.** Files are stored once, by hash, under their own file
name (installers read the format and the binary's name from it). The
four pinning backends download into the store and the file in
`downloads` is a hard link to it, so the archive takes no extra space;
across devices it falls back to a copy. I checked that these install
paths only read the downloaded file (raw binaries are copied and the
copy is made executable), and a stored file is hashed again before every
reuse, so an in-place change would cost a re-download, never a wrong
install. Partial downloads now resume from the store's staging area.

Turn it all off with `download_cache = false` (`MISE_DOWNLOAD_CACHE=0`).
The store holds up to 2 GiB, least recently used first.
`always_keep_download` is deprecated (warns from 2026.11.0, removed
2027.11.0): downloads are kept in the store instead.

**Trust.** The recorded hash lives beside the file, so it catches damage
but not a cache whose file and metadata were both replaced; without a
pinned checksum a writable cache is trusted, and the docs say so. The
extracted `http-tarballs` tree from `shared_extraction` (opt-in) is
still trusted as is.

**Docs.** A "Restored caches and installed tools" section in the
lockfile docs explains why mise can't validate an installed tree
(installs are mutable on purpose, and source-built tools differ from
their tarball) and what to do instead, with warnings on the `http`
shared-extraction note and the GitHub Actions section.

Tested with unit tests of the 304 path, a tampered stored file, pinned
reuse and the linked download, plus e2e tests for pinned and unpinned
reinstalls with the server stopped and a tampered entry. The http, aqua,
github and packslip e2e groups pass except
`test_http_compressed_binaries`, which fails here removing a system-wide
install under `/usr/local/share/mise`. Clippy with `-D warnings` is
clean.

feat(upgrade): add tool_update.global_auto to update every global tool (#14237)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/618
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Automatic tool updates were opt-in one tool at a time: every entry in
global config needed its own `auto_update = true`. The new
`tool_update.global_auto` setting turns them on for every tool in global
config at once. It takes the same values as `auto_update`: `true` checks
every `tool_update.check_duration` (24h by default), and a duration such
as `"12h"` sets the interval.

```toml
# ~/.config/mise/config.toml
[settings]
tool_update.global_auto = "12h"

[tools]
claude = "latest"                                   # checked every 12h
node = { version = "24", auto_update = "6h" }       # its own interval wins
python = { version = "3.13", auto_update = false }  # opted out
```

A tool's own `auto_update` takes precedence, so `auto_update = false`
opts a tool out. The existing rules still apply: only global (and
system) config counts, so a project can't set this, and a project's own
version of a tool is never updated. Exact versions such as `node =
"24.11.1"` stay put, and nothing updates offline, in CI, or with
`--locked`. `MISE_TOOL_UPDATE_GLOBAL_AUTO` sets it from the environment.

`self_update.auto` now accepts an interval too: `self_update.auto =
"1d"` checks for a new mise release every day, overriding
`self_update.check_duration`. `true` and `false` work as before.

### Also fixed

A global tool with `auto_update = false` used to create
`$MISE_STATE_DIR/tool-update` every time it launched, because the
service-lock check ran before the value was read. mise now reads the
value first and returns before touching the disk.

- New e2e `test_tool_update_global_auto`: `true` and an interval, shims,
the env var, a per-tool opt-out, exact versions, a project-set version,
and a project trying to turn the setting on.

still pass.
- Unit tests cover parsing a bool or an interval, and `self_update.auto
= "6h"` overriding `check_duration`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
passes.

fix(env): join adjacent quoted and unquoted dotenv value parts again (#14231)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/614
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

Since 2026.10.3, mise reads a dotenv value as exactly one of
single-quoted, double-quoted, or unquoted. Before that, values were read
like a shell word: quoted and unquoted parts next to each other were
joined and their quotes removed. Common `.env` lines broke:

```sh
A='it'\''s'
B=a'b c'd
C="one"'two'three
```

| | before 2026.10.3 | 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 | this PR |
|---|---|---|---|
| `A` | `it's` | syntax error | `it's` |
| `B` | `ab cd` | `a'b c'd` (quotes kept) | `ab cd` |
| `C` | `onetwothree` | syntax error | `onetwothree` |

The syntax error hurt most under the `env_file` setting
(`MISE_ENV_FILE=.env`): mise warned and dropped every line after `A`. In
`_.file`, it failed the whole config.

This PR joins value segments again, as before 2026.10.3. These stay the
same:

- Single-quoted parts are fully literal: no escapes, no `$VAR`
substitution (#14228).
- Variables resolve against the file's own earlier assignments first.
- A `${...}` expression is one unit, so quotes in a default (`${NAME:-"a
b"}`) don't split the value, and a brace inside a quoted default
(`${NAME:-"{}"}`) doesn't end the expression.

### Compatibility notes

- Quotes inside an unquoted value are now removed again. A JSON value
that must keep its quotes needs single quotes: `CONFIG='{"debug":
true}'`. Before 2026.10.3, `CONFIG={"debug":true}` gave `{debug:true}`;
2026.10.3–2026.10.6 kept the quotes. Unquoted JSON with spaces was a
syntax error before 2026.10.3, so files written for older mise are
unaffected.
- A quote partway through a value opens a quoted part only when its
partner comes later on the same line. Otherwise it's a literal
character, so `NAME=O'Brien` and `GREETING=it's great` read as written,
as they did in 2026.10.3–2026.10.6 (dotenvy rejected both). Only a
value's opening quote may span lines, as before. Quotes and comments are
read left to right, so a partner inside a trailing comment still counts
(as in dotenvy, `a'x #y'` is `ax #y`): write `NAME="O'Brien" # owner's
name`.
- Text after a closing quote is now part of the value (`KEY="a"b` gives
`ab`), so `mise_dotenv::ParseErrorKind::TrailingCharacters` no longer
occurs and is removed.

### Validation

- New unit tests cover concatenation, the quote/comment interactions,
substitution across segments, and dotenvy 0.15.7's own
`test_parse_value_escapes` cases (e.g. `KEY4='sweet $\fgs'\''fds'` →
`sweet $\fgs'fds`). Existing tests that asserted literal quotes in
unquoted values now expect dotenvy's results.
- `render_value` now quotes any value containing `'` or `"`. Its
round-trip property tests pass with 20,000 cases.
- New e2e test `e2e/env/test_env_file_quote_concatenation` covers
`_.file` and `MISE_ENV_FILE`. It fails without this change with the old
syntax error.
- A differential fuzz against dotenvy 0.15.7 compared ~936k single-line
values that dotenvy accepts. With the divergences that predate this PR
filtered out, the only difference left is a dotenvy quirk that keeps one
space before a comment after `$VAR`.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-features --all-targets -- -D warnings`
passes, and `cargo +1.95 check -p mise-dotenv` passes.

Divergences from dotenvy that predate this PR and are unchanged: an
unquoted `\n` stays a literal backslash-n (dotenvy wrote a newline), a
trailing lone `\` or `$` is kept (dotenvy dropped it), and `\ ` inside
double quotes is kept as written.

This branch is stacked on #14228 and includes its commit. Merge #14228
first; this diff then shrinks to the concatenation change.

fix(schema): accept task references in a task array (#14229)

A task written as an array can mix scripts with references to other
tasks, and mise runs them in order:

```toml
[tasks]
hello = "echo hello"
bye = "echo bye"
ci = ["echo first", { task = "hello" }, { task = "bye", args = [], env = { CI = "1" } }, { tasks = ["hello", "bye"] }]
```

The JSON schema allowed only strings in that array. So editors and
linters that use it, such as tombi or Taplo, flagged the tables as
errors even though `mise run ci` works. Each array item now uses the
same `task_run_entry` definition as a task's `run` key. That definition
allows a script string, `{ task, args, env }`, or a parallel `{ tasks =
[...] }` group. This is a schema change only, and mise's behavior does

fix(rust): treat rustup profile aliases like their full names (#14220)

rustup accepts `m`, `d` and `c` (and an empty value) for its `minimal`,
`default` and `complete` profiles, but mise compared the profile against
`"default"` literally. With

```toml
[tools]
rust = { version = "1.81.0", profile = "d" }
```

rustup installed the default profile. mise, though, did not count
clippy, rust-docs and rustfmt as required. So when one of them went
missing from the toolchain, `mise install` reported the tool as
installed and did not restore it. That restoring is the reconciliation
from #12771, and with `profile = "default"` it already worked.

mise now maps the aliases to the full names before it decides which
components the profile needs, matching rustup's own parser:

```rust
// rustup src/dist/mod.rs, impl FromStr for Profile
"minimal" | "m" => Ok(Self::Minimal),
"default" | "d" | "" => Ok(Self::Default),
"complete" | "c" => Ok(Self::Complete),
```

Only mise's own comparisons use the normalized name. rustup still
receives the profile as configured. An unknown profile name now fails in
mise with rustup's list of valid names, where before it reached rustup.

This takes over #12814 by @risu729, which pr-closer closed after 7 days
without contributor activity. Its CI had passed, and CodeRabbit and
Greptile had no findings. They are credited as co-author, and the change
is theirs, unchanged.

## Validation

- Unit test `profile_aliases_match_rustup` covers each full name, alias
and the empty value, plus an unknown name.
- `e2e/core/test_rust_components_reconcile` now installs with `profile =
"d"`, removes `rustfmt` from the toolchain, and checks that `mise
install` sees the gap and puts it back. It uses a fake `rustup`, so it
needs no network.
- Ran that e2e in Docker:
- With mise 2026.10.4, it fails at the new step. `mise install rust
--dry-run-code` reports `profile = "d"` as already installed with
`rustfmt` missing.
- With this PR's CI build on Ubuntu 24.04, it passes. `mise install`

feat(task): include working-tree changes in --affected and drop the experimental gate (#14214)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/607
<!-- entire-trail-link-end -->

`mise run --affected` only looked at committed changes, so you had to
commit before you could see which projects an edit touched. It now also
counts staged and unstaged edits and untracked files, so the selection
reflects what is in your working tree:

```sh
# Run build in projects changed by HEAD or by anything you have not committed yet
mise run --affected build

# Only what you have not committed yet
mise run --affected --affected-uncommitted --affected-untracked build

# Reproducible: the committed range only, as before
mise run --affected --affected-committed build
```

The three sources are `--affected-committed` (the `base...head` range),
`--affected-uncommitted` (staged and unstaged edits to tracked files,
against `HEAD`), and `--affected-untracked` (untracked files that
`.gitignore` does not exclude). With none of them, all three count.
Naming any of them limits the selection to those, and they combine. Each
also has an environment variable (`MISE_AFFECTED_COMMITTED`,
`MISE_AFFECTED_UNCOMMITTED`, `MISE_AFFECTED_UNTRACKED`).

- The working tree only counts when the head revision is the commit you

feat(dotfiles): add `mise dot save --re-encrypt` (#14210)

<!-- entire-trail-link-start -->
https://entire.io/gh/jdx/mise/trails/604

After you change `[history.encryption] recipients`, a save re-encrypts
only the files it reads from disk. Encrypted files the save carries
forward keep their old encryption: entries with `autosave = false` that
the save doesn't name, and variants for other platforms. A machine added
to the list then can't read them, and `mise bootstrap --adopt` fails
with `cannot unlock <path>` until each file is edited and saved again.

`mise dot save --re-encrypt` saves as usual, then re-encrypts every file
in the new checkpoint that was encrypted to a different recipient list:

```sh
mise dot save --re-encrypt
# mise history: re-encrypted 2 files to the current recipients
# mise history: saved checkpoint 3: re-encrypted 2 files to the current recipients
```

- It re-encrypts the **saved** version of each file. A manual-save
file's unsaved edits are never captured just to change its keys.
- If this machine can't unlock some files, nothing is saved, and the
error lists every one: ``cannot re-encrypt ~/.manual, ~/.other: no age
identity on this machine unlocks them; nothing was saved. Run `mise dot
save --re-encrypt` where they can be unlocked``
- With nothing to do, it prints `history: every encrypted file already
uses the current recipients` and records no checkpoint.
- Older checkpoints are not rewritten. As before, a machine added later
can only read versions saved after the change.

The "Change recipients" section of the encryption docs now explains
which files a plain save leaves behind and when to run `--re-encrypt`.

fix(storage): bound DocumentStore HTTP requests with a deadline (#1790)

* fix(storage): bound DocumentStore HTTP requests with a deadline

HttpDocumentStore issued every request without a deadline, so a request
whose peer never answers held its promise forever. The stage autosave
keeps at most one save in flight (startFlushRound's flushInFlight guard)
and starts the next one only once that promise settles, so a single
stalled save silently stranded every later save for the life of the page
— generation and the editor kept working from the in-memory store, and
the loss only surfaced on reload.

Bound the request round trip — sending the body and receiving the
response headers — with an AbortController deadline (requestTimeoutMs,
default 30s, <= 0 disables). A stalled request now rejects with
HttpDocumentStoreError(0, 'HTTP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT'), which the autosave's
existing backoff already retries. This mirrors the budget HttpAssetStore
applies via probeTimeoutMs / startBoundedOperation.

Reading the response body stays outside the bound: a large document on a
slow link is slow, not stalled.

commits.message:
Introduces an experimental GlideBuilder flag:
`setRespectExifOrientationInImageDecoder(boolean)`.

When enabled, InputStreamBitmapImageDecoderResourceDecoder and
ByteBufferBitmapImageDecoderResourceDecoder inspect EXIF orientation metadata
(via the new shared ExifOrientationOptionsApplier) and set
Downsampler.IS_EXIF_ORIENTATION_REQUIRED when rotation is needed.
DefaultOnHeaderDecodedListener uses this flag to configure ImageDecoder to use
ALLOCATOR_SOFTWARE instead of ALLOCATOR_HARDWARE, preventing redundant hardware
allocations and software canvas blit overhead on rotated captures.

Under the same flag, DefaultOnHeaderDecodedListener also raises the target size
passed to ImageDecoder#setTargetSize to at least one pixel per dimension, so
that very small requested sizes on highly elongated images cannot round down to
zero.

PiperOrigin-RevId: 996853280

Add an experimental fix for a race that leaves an in-use resource in the memory cache.

This race can cause the crash reported in https://github.com/bumptech/glide/issues/5782.

A resource is acquired before it is added to active resources, so an active resource normally has a count of at least 1. When the last holder releases it, the count drops to 0 first, and only then does `Engine.onResourceReleased()` remove it from active resources and move it to the memory cache. The decrement and the removal are two steps that no single lock protects.

In that short window, a load of the same key on another thread can find the resource in active resources with a count of 0 and acquire it again. The releasing thread then moves this in-use resource to the memory cache. When the cache evicts it, `recycle()` throws `IllegalStateException: Cannot recycle a resource while it is still acquired`.

The fix is behind a new experiment, `GlideBuilder.experimentalSetEnableActiveResourceReleaseRaceFix()`. With it on, `Engine.load()` acquires a resource from active resources only if its count is at least 1 (`EngineResource.acquireIfInUse()`), and otherwise treats the lookup as a miss.

Taking the `Engine` lock on the release path would also prevent this, but it can deadlock: a release can run while holding an `EngineJob` lock, and `Engine.load()` takes the `Engine` lock and then an `EngineJob` lock.

`EngineJobReleaseRaceTest` tests this race with the experiment on and off.

commits.message:
perf(relay): drop per-pulse ban reads and owner-link writes on HTTP (#8233)

## Why

Agents send an HTTP typing pulse (`POST /events`, kind 20002) every 3–5
seconds while they work. #8207 already routes the pulse's
write-restriction and serving checks through #8208's short-TTL caches.
Two per-pulse costs were still left at the membership step:

- **A fresh ban read** for the agent, plus its owner when the agent
comes in through NIP-OA (`deny_banned` → `community_ban_outcome`).
- **Four writer round-trips for owner-admitted agents**, on every
request: `materialize_nip_oa_owner` runs 2× `ensure_user` + the
`agent_owner_pubkey` upsert + an `is_agent_owner` confirm, even though
the link already exists.

## What changes

- **Typing's ban check reads the restriction cache.** `submit_event`
already parses the event before the membership step, so typing pulses
call a new `enforce_relay_membership_ephemeral`. Its ban check reads
through `restriction_state_cached`, the same 30s bound the pulse's
write-restriction check already has. Every other HTTP route, persistent
`POST /events`, and socket auth still read fresh (`cached: false`).
- **`materialize_nip_oa_owner` skips a link it already knows.** If
`observer_owner_cache` already holds `(community, agent, owner) = true`,
it returns `true` right away. `agent_owner_pubkey` has one production
writer, which sets it only `WHERE agent_owner_pubkey IS NULL`, and
nothing clears it, so the skipped writes were no-ops. This helps every
caller (HTTP, socket auth, audio). The owner-link disconnect only runs
on the first write, so it still runs.
- **`observer_owner_cache` capacity goes from 1k to 100k**, so
concurrently active agents actually hit it. That's tens of MB per pod at
most, the same scale as `restriction_cache`.

Per-pulse Postgres work at the membership step:

| Agent | Before | After |
|---|---|---|
| Direct relay member | host lookup (writer) + membership + ban | host
lookup (writer) + membership |
| Owner-admitted (NIP-OA) | host lookup + 2 memberships + 2 bans + 4
writer trips | host lookup + 2 memberships |

## Not in this PR

- **Caching host → community.** It's the tenant-binding step every HTTP
request goes through, and it reads from the writer. Community deletion
depends on new requests not binding once a community leaves `active`. A
cache would keep binding a quiescing community for its TTL. The
serving-write leases may make that harmless, but that needs a closer
look than a "safe fixes" PR.
- **Caching relay membership.** Removing a member has no HTTP equivalent
of the socket disconnect, so a cache would delay removal by its TTL.
- **The desktop client reusing one connection.** That's going in a
separate buzz-app PR.

## Unrelated one-liner

The `sadscan` pre-commit hook scans whole staged files. It blocked this
commit on a pre-existing test-only URI in `handlers/auth.rs`
(`postgres://buzz:buzz_dev@127.0.0.1:1/buzz`, a deliberately unreachable
stub). I added the hook's own `// sadscan:disable np.postgres.1` marker
to that line.

removed:
- `typing_ban_gate_uses_cached_restriction_row`: a member banned in
Postgres with a cached clear row can still type. Fails if typing reads
fresh.
- `persistent_post_ban_gate_reads_fresh`: a stale cached ban doesn't
refuse a kind-9 post that Postgres allows. Fails if every kind reads the

feat(relay): accept typing indicators over HTTP POST /events (#8207)

## Summary

Agents hosted inside the Buzz app sign their own events but don't hold a
WebSocket, so they couldn't show "typing…" in a channel. `POST /events`
rejected kind 20002 (typing indicator) with `restricted: unknown event
kind`.

Now, when `POST /events` receives a kind 20002 event, the bridge passes
it to the same channel broadcast the WebSocket path uses. Live
subscribers in the channel get the pulse. Nothing is written to
Postgres.

Before broadcasting, the relay checks, in order:
- the event has an `h` tag naming the channel
- the serialized event is at most 2 KiB (real typing events are ~600
bytes). Measuring the whole JSON, not just content and tag values, means
piling on empty tags can't get around the cap
- the signature and id are valid
- bans and timeouts
- the community write fence (over HTTP, a quiescing community's host
already fails to bind with a 404, so this catches quiescing that starts
after the tenant is bound)
- the sender is a channel member, or the channel is open (same rule as
WebSocket)
- the signer is the pubkey that authenticated the request (checked
first; a mismatch returns 403)

The existing HTTP admission rate limit and relay-membership gate still
run before any of this. Other ephemeral kinds are still rejected over
HTTP. `publish_channel_ephemeral` is the old WebSocket channel-broadcast
code moved into a shared helper, so both paths use the same membership
check and fan-out.

Unlike the WebSocket path, HTTP requires the `h` tag. Over WebSocket, a
20002 with no channel goes to every subscriber.

Points left for review:
- HTTP typing pulses count against the same per-pubkey HTTP quota as
message posts (default 300/min). One pulse every 3 s is 20/min per
active channel.
- A failed Redis publish is logged and the POST still returns `accepted:
true`, same as the WebSocket path. A pulse is resent every 3 s and
expires after 8 s, so a retry would only resend a stale pulse.

The `sadscan:disable` comment on an existing test URL in `ingest.rs` is
there because the secret scanner reads every file a commit touches. It
uses the same form as the other local test fixtures in the repo.

### Related issue

Needed for Agents2 typing indicators in buzz-app. The client PR depends
on this one and will follow as a draft.

### Testing

- 9 new Postgres-backed tests in `api/typing_postgres_tests.rs` cover
these cases: a member's pulse is published and not stored; a non-member
gets a 400; a timed-out member gets a 403; a signer mismatch gets a 403;
a missing `h` tag gets a 400; a tampered event gets a 400; kind 20001 is
still rejected; oversized events get a 400 (2 KiB of content, one 2 KiB
tag value, or `h` + 10k empty tags); a community that starts quiescing
after the tenant is bound gets a 400 `community writes are fenced`, and
nothing is published. Two mutation checks: with the fence removed, the
fence test fails; with the old content-plus-tag-values cap, the
empty-tags case is accepted and the test fails.

- buzz-relay unit tests pass (1476). One mesh demo test timed out once

notes](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/push-capability-v1/docs/buzz-push.md)

perf(relay): cache ephemeral-path serving and restriction reads (#8208)

## Summary

Typing pulses and agent observer frames each ran two Postgres reads on
the WebSocket path in `handlers/event.rs`: whether the community still
serves writes (`is_serving_active`), and the sender's ban/timeout row
(`moderation_restriction_state`). Both now read through short-TTL moka
caches on `AppState`, following the membership cache's pattern.

- **Serving state, keyed per community, 10 s TTL.** Every typer in a
community shares one entry, so a pod does about one read per community
per 10 s.
- **Raw restriction row, keyed per (community, pubkey), 30 s TTL.** It
caches the row, not the verdict, so the verdict is still taken at "now"
and a cached timeout lifts the second it ends. One exception: `banned`
is computed when the row is read, so a ban with an expiry can outlast
that expiry by up to the TTL.
- **The TTL is the staleness bound.** On every pod, and for every way a
ban or timeout changes (signed commands, the admin API, report
resolution, an owner's moderation reaching their agents), the ephemeral
path sees the change within 30 s (10 s for archive/delete). As a best
effort, signed ban/unban/timeout/untimeout (9040–9043) also drop the
target's own entry on the pod that handles the command. Bans also keep
their existing cluster-wide socket disconnect, and archiving a community
disconnects all of its sockets.
- **Hit/miss counters** `buzz_serving_active_cache_{hits,misses}_total`
and `buzz_restriction_cache_{hits,misses}_total`, matching the
membership cache, so the saved reads can be confirmed in prod.
- **The durable fence stays uncached.** Persistent ingest, moderation
commands, auth, and NIP-43 leave (28936, ephemeral-range but ingested)
still read Postgres directly. The worst staleness case is a
just-timed-out user's typing dots or observer frames getting through on
another pod for up to 30 s. Real messages are never affected.

### Related issue
N/A. This is the ephemeral-path Postgres read cost raised in the
typing-indicator load discussion. Searched for existing PRs and found
none.

### Testing
- New Postgres tests:
- The ephemeral gate honours a cached ban and admits an expired cached
timeout.
  - The ephemeral fence honours a cached "fenced" community.
  - A cache miss fills both caches.
- At the `handle_event` seam, a stored write (kind 1) is accepted
despite a cached ban or a cached "fenced" state, and NIP-43 leave skips
the cached ban. Mutation-checked: switching either ingest check to its
cached variant, or dropping the 28936 carve-out, turns one red.
- Timeout and untimeout commands drop the cached row. Mutation-checked:
removing the invalidation turns it red.
- Live test on a local relay: 100 typing pulses made 0
restriction/serving reads; 10 real messages made 10 of each. A timeout
written straight to the DB refused messages at once and typing after ~30
s; an archive written straight to the DB fenced typing after ~10 s.
- `scripts/postgres-test-run.sh -p buzz-relay --lib --tests`: 384/384
passed (local PG14).
- `cargo nextest run -p buzz-relay --lib --tests`: 1470 passed. The 6
`api::media` failures are environmental: those tests seed through the
default `:5432` database, which locally has no `buzz` role.
- `cargo clippy -p buzz-relay --all-targets -D warnings` is clean.
- Review follow-up commit pushed with the full pre-push hook passing.

fix(push): isolate push enqueue and stop workers on rollback (#8216)

Push enqueueing previously ran inside the message transaction, so a push
lock or database error could block or reject a message. Configured relay
writers now submit bounded best-effort work only after commit. A
dedicated connection and bounded queue isolate enqueue waits and
failures from message-write connections. Overload, errors, process loss,
or shutdown may drop a notification; the committed message remains
authoritative.

`BUZZ_PUSH_ENABLED=false` disables the application producer and workers.
Updated writer connections always bypass any surviving enqueue trigger.
The overlap migration updates an existing function without resurrecting
retired objects. Apply it before relying on isolation with a surviving
trigger, and replace every old enabled process and writer connection:
missing settings preserve legacy behavior during overlap.

SIGTERM/Ctrl-C cancels enqueue, matcher, and delivery work before
listener drain. Durable queues, claims, leases, preferences, and
delivery configuration remain intact. Claims expire normally; gateway
requests already accepted may still deliver. Reactivation requires an
explicit operator decision about retained work. There is no automatic
purge, startup interlock, or backfill of messages written while
disabled.

Built on merged [#8135](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/8135),
including [#8178](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/8178). Trigger
retirement [#8210](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/8210) remains
open; this change is tested with the trigger present and after removal.
Operational details are in [the rollback and reactivation
guide](https://github.com/block/buzz/blob/relay-push-rollback/docs/push-gateway-deployment.md#relay-rollback-and-reactivation).

Requests and responses take the new shape, so the client integration can

```
→ { channels: [channel], next_cursor }
channel: { channel_id, unread: bool, mentions, read_through_id|null, latest_id|null, threads: [thread] }
thread:  { root_id, unread: bool, mentions, read_through_id|null, latest_id }

POST /buzz/v1/me/read-state
{ intents: [{ type: "mark_through", target: { channel_id [, root_id] }, message_id }] }
→ { outcomes: [applied|blocked|invalid|unknown], channels: [channel] }
```

What changed and why:
- **Channel and thread positions are fully separate.** Channel
`unread`/`mentions` count only top-level messages. Thread replies count
only on their thread row. `mark_channel_read` and its whole-channel cut
are gone. "Mark channel read" sends a channel `mark_through` at
`latest_id`, plus one per thread row to clear threads too.
- **Channel `latest_id` is always a top-level message.** It used to be
able to point at a reply, and a channel `mark_through` rejects a reply
as its anchor. It also skips a reply-marked message whose ancestry never
resolved, because marking through one would fail on every retry.
- **`read_through_id`:** frontiers stored only the anchor's arrival
time. Migration 0058 adds `personal_read_frontiers.through_message_id`,
which follows the greatest arrival, and drops the now-unused
`threads_through_timestamp`. This is the only storage change.
- **Counts are plain numbers.** The exact/at_least/unknown wrappers are
gone. Evidence the relay can't use (unusable tags, unresolved ancestry,
undecided conversation membership, past the scan cap) leaves the message
out, so counts can undercount.
- **POST returns the updated row** of each distinct channel it applied
to, so the client doesn't refetch after every read. If those rows can't
be read after the writes commit, `channels` is omitted and the outcomes
still stand. The row refresh shares the 8 s intent deadline.
- **Up to 25 thread rows per channel** (was 5). Five hid a mention in a
sixth unread thread. 25 is the most that keeps a POST's rows for
`MAX_INTENTS` (100) channels inside the 1 MiB response limit; 50 would
be ~1.4 MB, a 503 that hides already-committed outcomes. A unit test
builds that worst-case response and fails if the cap outgrows the limit.
- **The doc separates shape from behavior.** `/buzz/v1` promises a
stable shape (fields, types, status variants, what `mark_through` does).
What the counts include (which messages are unread or directed, which
threads are listed, the bounds) may change while v1 is pre-release, so
clients replace their rows with each response instead of reconciling
against local counts.
- **Removed from the wire:** the explicit-contexts read (`GET
/me/read-state?targets=`), `account`, channel name/type/archived/hidden
(these come from Nostr metadata), `latest_message_at`/`_complete`, and
the NIP-11 `max_contexts`/`max_context_messages`/`max_thread_summaries`.

Deliberately deferred (behavior or additive, no shape change):
- Thread counting rule (relay counts a reply if you wrote or replied to
its direct parent; the client uses "posted anywhere in the thread or
followed"), the workflow-owner attribution p-tag, and thread-row
`mentions` counting every counted reply rather than directed ones.
- `follow`/`unfollow` intents, listing followed threads that are already
read, and a truncation flag for the thread list.

fix(desktop): repair the Windows notification shim's false denial on read (#5600)

Addresses #2445. Closely related to #2483 -- see "Relationship to #2483"
below; I am happy to close this in favour of that one.

## The problem

On Windows the notification plugin's injected shim decides its
permission at startup like this
([`guest-js/init.ts:12-18`](https://github.com/tauri-apps/plugins-workspace/blob/v2/plugins/notification/guest-js/init.ts)):

```ts
if (window.Notification.permission !== 'default' || __TEMPLATE_windows__) {
  return await Promise.resolve(window.Notification.permission === 'granted')
}
return await invoke('plugin:notification|is_permission_granted')
```

`__TEMPLATE_windows__` is replaced with the literal `true` on Windows,
so the `||` short-circuits and the shim compares its own
freshly-initialised `'default'` against `'granted'` -- `false` -- and
stamps **`denied`**. The line that would ask the backend is unreachable,
and the backend would have said yes: `permission_state()` returns
`PermissionState::Granted` unconditionally on desktop.

So on every launch of the Windows app, `window.Notification.permission`
is `denied` and nothing in the OS is denying anything.

## Why the toggle is only half of it

`getDesktopNotificationPermissionState()` trusts that value, so
`refreshPermission()` reports `denied` at mount, and this effect in
`hooks.ts` runs before the user touches anything:

```ts
React.useEffect(() => {
  if (settings.desktopEnabled && (permission === "denied" || permission === "unsupported")) {
    setSettings((current) => ({ ...current, desktopEnabled: false }));
  }
}, [permission, settings.desktopEnabled]);
```

It writes `desktopEnabled: false` and persists it. Measured on a real
install: with alerts successfully enabled and `desktopEnabled` persisted
as `true`, a clean relaunch comes back with it persisted as `false`.

That means fixing only the enable path leaves a Windows user re-enabling
alerts after every restart.

## What this changes

One place: `getDesktopNotificationPermissionState()` repairs the bogus
value instead of reporting it.

```ts
if (
  window.Notification.permission === "denied" &&
  isTauri() &&
  isWindowsPlatform()
) {
  try {
    return await requestDesktopNotificationAccess();
  } catch {
    return window.Notification.permission;
  }
}
```

`requestPermission()` is the only call that reaches the backend, and on
Windows it raises no prompt, returns `Granted`, and rewrites the shim's
cached value -- so this is self-limiting: the next read short-circuits
as `granted` and never requests again. There is a test for exactly that.

Repairing at the read rather than at the toggle fixes every consumer at
once, including `sendDesktopNotification()`, which gates delivery on
`=== "granted"` and would otherwise drop notifications at boot.

- `denied` stays terminal on macOS, on Linux, and on ordinary Windows
web pages.
- A denial that survives the request is still reported as `denied`.
- A rejected request falls back to the current value instead of
propagating; callers do not handle rejections today.
- Adds `isWindowsPlatform()` to `shared/lib/platform.ts`, alongside the
existing `isMacPlatform()` / `isLinuxPlatform()`.
- No new dependencies. No changes to `hooks.ts` or to notification
delivery.

## Verification on a real Windows 11 install

Buzz Desktop 0.5.9 release build, Windows 11 Home 10.0.26200, WebView2
151.0.4129.72, attached over CDP. Clean boot, nothing injected:

```
window.Notification.permission                -> "denied"
localStorage[...].desktopEnabled              -> false      (written by the effect above)

await window.Notification.requestPermission() -> "granted"
window.Notification.permission                -> "granted"

new window.Notification("Buzz", { body: ... })
ToastNotificationManager::History
  .GetHistory("xyz.block.buzz.app")           -> 3 -> 4     (real toast delivered)
CreateToastNotifier(...).Setting              -> Enabled
```

The OS was permissive throughout: no `ToastEnabled` override, no
notification policy keys under HKCU or HKLM, and the app present under
`HKCU\...\Notifications\Settings\xyz.block.buzz.app`. Full detail in
[this
comment](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/2483#issuecomment-5255972424).

To be precise about scope: this confirms the mechanism the patch relies
on, measured on a stock release build. The patched build itself is
covered by the unit tests below, not by a packaged Windows run.

## Tests

`pnpm test` -- full desktop suite. New cases in `lib/desktop.test.mjs`:

- Windows Tauri repairs the shim's false denied state on read
- the repaired state is cached, so later reads do not request again
- a denial that survives the request is reported as denied
- denied stays terminal outside the Windows Tauri app (Windows web,
Linux Tauri, Linux web)
- granted is returned untouched and never triggers a request

Plus `shared/lib/platform.test.mjs` for `isWindowsPlatform()` across
`Win32` / `Win64` / `Windows` and `MacIntel` / `Darwin` / `Linux
x86_64`.

## Relationship to #2483

#2483 fixes the same root cause at the toggle: it retries the request
inside `setDesktopEnabled`. That makes the toggle work, which is what
#2445 reports, and its `ensureDesktopNotificationPermission` helper is a
nicer shape than an inline condition.

The difference is where the repair happens. Because #2483 leaves the
mount-time read as `denied`, the effect quoted above still turns the
setting off on every launch, so the fix does not survive a restart.
Repairing at the read covers the toggle path too, since
`setDesktopEnabled` calls `refreshPermission()` first and finds
`granted`.

The two overlap: both add `isWindowsPlatform()` to `platform.ts`, so
whichever lands second needs a trivial rebase. If maintainers prefer
#2483's shape, the equivalent of this PR is to call its helper from
`refreshPermission` as well as from `setDesktopEnabled` -- I am glad to
close this and send that instead. I did not want to push changes into
someone else's open PR uninvited.

## Once this lands

#2445 can close. I am running a per-machine launcher workaround for a
small Windows team until then, which this makes unnecessary.

fix(mobile): normalize relay URL before disabling push (#8201)

Communities joined with a `ws://` or `wss://` relay URL cannot disable
push: the opt-out path passes that URL directly to the HTTP-only NIP-11
fetcher, fails before publishing the inactive lease, and leaves the
durable retry pending. This was reproduced in USB logs from TestFlight
0.20.1 (49).

Normalize the URL with the existing push relay HTTP helper before
fetching metadata, matching the revocation outbox's handling. No
settings UI changes. Related: #8199 removes the status text but does not
fix this synchronization failure; no duplicate fix found.

### Validation

Four regression cases exercise the real community deactivator through
its HTTP boundary. The WebSocket cases fail with the device's exact
exception before the fix; all four pass afterward. All 37 focused
community/revocation tests and targeted Flutter analysis pass. An
initial full mobile run had three failures (recount timing and native
export timeout/order); all three passed in isolated reruns. The full
mobile checks and test suite passed on retry. The local repository-wide
gate stopped during Rust compilation without a final result; a full
local pass is not claimed. [GitHub
CI](https://github.com/block/buzz/actions/runs/37865048873) passed,
including mobile tests, Android build, Swift tests, iOS simulator build,
and unsigned iOS release build. [Codex
review](https://github.com/block/buzz/pull/8201#issuecomment-6071795750)
reported no major issues.

The installed TestFlight build is unchanged. After this fix lands,
validate that upgrading the same installation clears its existing
pending opt-out and leaves the relay lease inactive, without toggling
notifications back on.
